Gas Transport by the Blood
We now consider the respiratory gases, oxygen and carbon dioxide, which are carried
by the blood. First we’ll look at oxygen, including the dissociation curve and factors
that affect the oxygen affinity of hemoglobin. Then we’ll look at carbon dioxide, which
is carried in the blood in three forms.
I. Oxygen transport
O2 is carried in the blood in two forms: (1) dissolved and (2) combined with
hemoglobin (chemically bound).
a. Dissolved O2
O2 that is dissolved in the blood obeys Henry’s law, that is, the amount of O2
dissolved is proportional to the partial pressure and the O2 solubility (see figure). For
each mm Hg of PO2 there is 0.003 ml O2 per 100 ml of blood (0.003 vol %). Thus
normal arterial blood with a PO2 of 100 mm Hg contains 3 ml O2 in a liter of blood in
dissolved form.
With a normal cardiac output of 5 liters/min, the total amount of dissolved O2 which is
delivered to the tissues is only 5 x 3 = 15 ml/min. It is easy to see that this way of
transporting O2 is inadequate, because tissues consumption of O2 at rest is
approximately 300 ml/min and increases to 3000 ml/min during exercise. Clearly, an
additional method of transporting O2 is required. This small amount of dissolved O2 is
not important from a quantitative point of view, but it is very important for the transfer
of O2 through all solutions or membranes. Only in dissolved form can O2 diffuse
through alveoli-capillary membranes and blood plasma in the lung or through cell
membranes and cytoplasm of the cells in tissues. Dissolved oxygen can also become
important during oxygen therapy, especially by hyperbaric oxygen treatment.

b. Oxygen combined with hemoglobin (chemically bound O2)
Heme is an iron-porphyrin compound, which is joined to the protein globin and
consists of four polypeptide chains. The chains are of two types, alpha and beta, and
differences in their amino acid sequences give rise to various types of human
hemoglobin. Normal adult hemoglobin is known as Hemoglobin A.
O2 forms an easily reversible combination with hemoglobin (Hb) to produce
oxyhemoglobin:
O2 + Hb
HbO2
The O2 concentration in the blood is related to the PO2 of the blood and depends on
the hemoglobin concentration. The figure shows the relationship between oxygen
concentration and pressure for a normal hemoglobin concentration (O2 dissociation
curve). Total O2 content is displayed by the non-linear curve and dissolved O2 by the
straight line. The concentration of O2 combined with hemoglobin (HbO2) can be
calculated as the difference between total and dissolved O2 concentrations. Note that
the amount of O2 carried by the Hb increases rapidly up to a PO2 of about 50 mm Hg,
but above that the curve becomes much flatter.
The maximum amount of O2 that can be combined with Hb is called the O2 capacity.
This is when all of the available binding sites are occupied by O2. Therefore, O2
capacity depends only on hemoglobin concentration. One gram of pure Hb can
combine with 1.34 ml O2, and because normal blood has about 15 gm of Hb / 100 ml,
the O2 capacity is about 20.1 ml O2 / 100 ml of blood.

Relationship between dissolved O2 and hemoglobin bound O2:
The partial pressure of O2 is produced only by dissolved molecules, but there
is always a dynamic relationship between dissolved and chemically bounded
molecules.
The higher the dissolved O2 concentration and thus the PO2, the greater would
be the O2 concentration combined with hemoglobin. Driving force for O2
diffusion through biological barriers is always the O2 partial pressure difference
between the two sites. As dissolved O2 molecules are diffusing away from a
location and causing PO2 to fall, O2 bounded molecules are set free to
enhance the pressure for further diffusion. Equilibrium is then achieved only by
the equality of O2 partial pressures (and not by equality of O2 concentrations)
between the two sites of the barrier.

O2 saturation of Hb: is defined as the percentage of the available hemoglobin
binding sites that have O2 attached, and is given by:
O2 combined with Hb/O2 Capacity
The O2 Saturation is plotted against PO2 in the figure below (a saturation of 1.0 in the
graph means 100 % saturation).
It is important to note that this curve does not
include the physically dissolved O2. As seen in the figure, the O2 saturation of arterial
blood with a PO2 of 100 mm Hg is about 98%, whereas that of mixed venous blood
with a PO2 of 40 mm Hg is about 75 %.
The O2 saturation is 50 % at a PO2 of 27 mm Hg. This PO2 is called P50 (or P0.5) and
is a measure for the affinity of hemoglobin for O2.
The curved-shape of the O2 dissociation curve has several physiological advantages:
The flat upper portion means that even if the PO2 in alveolar gas falls slightly (for
example in diseases or by climbing to high altitudes) loading of the blood with O2 will
only be mildly affected. The steep lower part of the dissociation curve means that the
peripheral tissues can withdraw large amount of O2 for only a small drop in capillary
PO2. This maintenance of blood PO2 assists the diffusion of O2 into the tissue cells
(driving force for O2 diffusion is PO2 difference between capillary and tissue).

II. O2 Affinity and O2 Delivery:
The O2 saturation of hemoglobin is plotted against PO2 in the oxygen 
dissociation curve (see figure). The affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen is 
represented by the P50. The P50 is defined as the partial pressure of O2 
required to achieve 50% hemoglobin saturation.  The normal value, at 37° C 
and pH 7.4, is 27 mm Hg (red curve in middle). If the P50 is less than 27 mm 
Hg, then hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen (binds more easily), and 
the dissociation curve shifts to the left (green curve). A right shift (high P50) 
indicates a lower affinity for oxygen (blue curve).

III. Factors That Influence P50:
a. Hydrogen ion: As [H+] changes, O2 affinity changes because hydrogen ions
bind reversibly to the imidazole group of the amino acid histidine.
High [H+]
shifts the equilibrium and dissociation curve to the right.
Low [H+] shifts the
equilibrium and the curve to the left. This relationship was first described by
Christian Bohr in 1904 and is known as the Bohr Effect.
b. Carbon dioxide also affects the O2 affinity. High PCO2 lowers the affinity
(right shift) by two mechanisms. First, CO2 binds to the N-terminus of the alpha
and beta chains of hemoglobin reducing hemoglobin affinity for O2, and
second, increasing CO2 concentration causes an increase in hydrogen ions
which in turn decrease the O2 affinity (indirect effect).

Summary slide for Factors That Influence P50:
a. Hydrogen ion: As [H+] changes, O2 affinity changes because hydrogen ions bind reversibly to the
imidazole group of the amino acid histidine. High [H+] shifts the equilibrium and dissociation curve to the
right. Low [H+] shifts the equilibrium and the curve to the left. This relationship was first described by
Christian Bohr in 1904 and is known as the Bohr Effect.
b. Carbon dioxide also affects the O2 affinity. High PCO2 lowers the affinity (right shift) by two
mechanisms. First, CO2 binds to the N-terminus of the alpha and beta chains of hemoglobin reducing
hemoglobin affinity for O2, and second, increasing CO2 concentration causes an increase in hydrogen
ions which in turn decrease the O2 affinity (indirect effect).
c. Temperature will also change the affinity for O2. High temperature decreases affinity.
d. 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG or BPG) alters the affinity for O2 by reversibly binding to the beta
chains of hemoglobin.
An increase in 2,3-DPG shifts the curve to the right. An increase in the
concentration of this material occurs in chronic hypoxia, for example, at high altitude or in the presence
of chronic lung disease. As a result, the unloading of O2 to peripheral tissues is assisted.
e. Type of hemoglobin – variations in amino acid sequence produce Hb variants that usually have
altered O2 affinity; e.g. fetal hemoglobin has a much higher affinity than maternal Hb.
The affinity of hemoglobin is a compromise between the need to load O2 at the lung and the need to
unload O2 at the tissues. Ideally, a high affinity is preferable when blood enters the lung to load oxygen,
and a low affinity is preferable when blood enters the tissues to unload oxygen. In fact, because of the
chemical factors listed above, the affinity changes between lungs and tissues. This occurs because as
CO2 leaves the blood and pH rises in lung capillaries, there is a slight left shift in the dissociation curve,
facilitating O2 loading, and as CO2 enters the capillary at the tissues, there is a slight right shift in the
dissociation curve, facilitating O2 unloading. In exercising muscle, the unloading is further facilitated by
lower pH and higher temperature.

IV. Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
Carbon monoxide (CO) interferes with the O2 transport function of the blood by combining with Hb to form
carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). Carbon monoxide and O2 bind reversibly to the same site on the hemoglobin
molecule. CO has about 240 times the affinity of O2 for Hb; this means that CO will combine with the
same amount of Hb as O2 when the CO partial pressure is 240 times lower.
If alveolar gas contains only 0.1% CO, then 50% of hemoglobin binding sites will be loaded with CO. For
this reason, small amounts of CO can tie up a large proportion of Hb in the blood, thus making it
unavailable to carry O2.
The figure shows the O2 dissociation curves for the blood with a normal Hb concentration (orange curve
on top), or with a half Hb concentration (blue curve on bottom) and also for the blood that has a normal
Hb concentration, but 50% of its Hb is loaded with CO (green curve in middle). Note that the curve with
50% CO loading is shifted to the left compared to the curve with the half concentration of Hb. This means
the presence of COHb shifts the O2 dissociation curve to the left, thus interfering with the unloading of O2.
This is an additional feature of the toxicity of CO. The tetrameric structure of Hb undergoes a
conformational change when CO is bound at one of the four heme sites, with a resulting increase in the
affinity of the remaining heme groups for oxygen. This increase in O2 affinity reduces unloading of O2 in
the tissues.
Cigarette smokers (pack a day) have about 5% of their Hb combined with CO.
During CO poisoning, Hb concentration and PO2 of the blood may be normal, but the O2 concentration is
grossly reduced. Blood PO2 remains normal because the alveolar CO fraction that could create a severe
HbCO poisoning is still too small (0.001 by 0.1% inhaled CO) to reduce the inspired O2 fraction.
Therefore, no significant change in alveolar PO2 would occur. High levels of CO in the air would certainly
lower alveolar PO2 just like any other gas in the alveoli, but living at such a level of CO is not possible.
Severe CO poisoning may require blood transfusions or treatment of the patient with hyperbaric oxygen.
Hyperbaric treatment is effective since both O2 and CO compete for the heme binding sites, and a high
PO2 would drive CO off the binding sites and allow O2 to bind

V. Oxidation of hemoglobin (Methemoglobin):
Another inactive form of hemoglobin is oxidized hemoglobin. If the normal
heme iron (Fe++) is oxidized by some oxidizing substances to Fe+++ form, it
loses its O2 binding capability and is unable to carry O2. (Figure right side).
This type of hemoglobin with oxidized iron is called Methemoglobin. Some
hemoglobin molecules undergo oxidation each day, but they are converted
back to normal hemoglobin by the plasma methemoglobin reductase. The
oxygen carriage capacity of a patient with a methemoglobin reductase
deficiency is significantly reduced.
It is important to note that the oxidation of Hb (right side of figure) is different
from oxygenation of Hb (left side of figure). During oxygenation (O2 loading)
and deoxygenation (O2 unloading) processes there is no change in the
valence of iron and it maintains its (Fe ++) form.

VI. CO2 Transport
CO2 is carried in the blood in three forms: (1) Physically dissolved, (2) as
bicarbonate, and (3) in combination with proteins such as carbamino
compounds.
1) Dissolved CO2: like O2, dissolved CO2 obeys Henry’s law, but CO2 is about
20 times more soluble than O2, its solubility being 0.067 ml / dl x mm Hg. As a
result, dissolved CO2 plays a significant role in its transport, since about 10 %
of CO2 is transported in this form.

When the concentration of these ions rise within the red cell, H+ is buffered by

3) Carbamino compounds: are formed by combination of CO2 with terminal

The most important protein is the globin of hemoglobin. Deoxygenated
hemoglobin can bind more CO2 as carbamino-hemoglobin than oxygenated
Hb. Thus, unloading of O2 in peripheral capillaries facilitates loading of CO2,
whereas oxygenation in the lung has the opposite effect (Haldane effect).
About 20% of the total CO2 carried in the blood occurs in this form.

2. Haldane effect: The effect of O2 on CO2 and H+ in combination with
proteins is the Haldane Effect. Increases in PO2 reduce the combination of
both CO2 and H+ with hemoglobin. This effect facilitates CO2 loading in the
tissue capillaries and CO2 unloading in the lung. Therefore, O2 causes a right
shift in CO2 binding curve.
Bohr and Haldane effects:
The effects of CO2 and H+ on the O2 affinity of hemoglobin are the Bohr
Effect. Increases in both CO2 and H+ cause a decrease in O2 affinity of Hb.
This effect assists O2 loading in the lung and O2 unloading in the system
capillaries, whereas Haldane effect assists CO2 loading in system capillaries
and CO2 unloading in the lung

KEY CONCEPTS
1.
Most of the O2 transported in the blood is bound to 
hemoglobin. The maximum amount that can be bound is called 
the O2 capacity. The O2 saturation is the amount combined with 
hemoglobin divided by the capacity and is equal to the 
proportion of the binding sites that are occupied by O2. 
2.
The O2 dissociation curve is shifted to the right (that is, the O2
affinity of the hemoglobin is reduced) by increases in PCO2, H+, 
temperature, and 2,3-Biphosphoglycerate. 
3.
Most of the CO2 in the blood is in the form of bicarbonate, with 
smaller amounts as dissolved and carbamino compounds. 
4.
The CO2 dissociation curve is much steeper and more linear 
than that for O2. 
5.
The PO2 in some tissues is less than 5 mm Hg, and the purpose 
of the much higher PO2 in the capillary blood is to provide an 
adequate gradient for diffusion. Factors determining O2
delivery to tissues include the blood O2 concentration and the 
blood flow.
